newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan court sentences serial child-killer to death.
newsitem.headline: Japan court sentences serial child-killer to death.

text.p: A Japanese court sentenced a serial killer to death on Monday for the gruesome kidnap-murders of four small girls.

Tsutomo Miyazaki's brutal acts shocked Japan. He mailed the remains of one of the girls to her family, ate dismembered body parts, drank the blood of one of the victims and took video footage of the body parts.
Presiding Judge Kenjiro Tao of the Tokyo District Court convicted Miyazaki of abducting and murdering the girls, aged between four and seven, in 1988 and 1989 and sentenced him to death by hanging.

"The defendant's motive was sexual desire and could only be described as shameless," Tao said. "This is a heinous crime violating human dignity and there is no choice but to hand down the death sentence."
It took the court seven years to determine whether Miyazaki, 34, a former printing shop assistant, was sane.
He went through three psychiatric examinations, all of which showed different results.

Tao said the court accepted the first examination which concluded that Miyazaki had some personality defects but was not mentally ill. The other two said Miyazaki was suffering from multiple personalities or schizophrenia, which should be mitigating factors.
Japan has no jury system. The death penalty is usually handed down to perpetrators of premeditated murder.

Miyazaki was caught in July 1989 by the father of a six-year-old girl, a would-be fifth victim, having tried to confuse the investigation by writing letters to local media in the name of a fictitious woman.
Police later found Miyazaki's room full of paedophile films and magazines as well as the videotapes of dismembered body parts of the girls he killed.
Throughout his trial, Miyazaki remained indifferent to the court proceedings and made incoherent remarks.
When asked in court what led him to his actions, Miyazaki said: "A mouse-man appeared every time the girls started crying, I think all these things took place in a dream."
Miyazaki's lawyers said they would appeal the ruling, based on the discrepancies between the three psychiatric tests.

The appeal means Miyazaki will not be immediately sent to death row. The controversial nature of the three examinations and his own remarks in court mean the session at the Tokyo High Court could take several more years.
Shinobu Yoshioka, an author who has followed the case since the first murders, said he doubted the validity of Monday's ruling.
"If he were truly normal, he wouldn't have eaten fingers or drunk the blood of victims," Yoshioka said.
But another legal affairs expert, author Ryuzo Saki, disagreed.
"I respect the court's seven-year observation of the defendant," he said.
Japan suspended executions in November 1989 but resumed them in March 1993. Activists say 18 death row convicts have since been hanged.
"This ruling appears to be a response to calls for abolishing capital punishment," said Akira Fukushima, psychology professor at Sophia University. "I think there is a political motive behind it."
